A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DEER. Their main texts, appendices, figures, tables, and equations are readable and support reliable matching despite the changed title, terminology, and organization.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, human–LLM agreement measurements, and claim-extraction and verification experiments in Section 6 and Appendices F–G.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark and human-agreement results, revised module evaluations, and additional adversarial verification experiments in Appendix F.

M1.justification: The hybrid architecture and semantic backtracking remain, but the reported rubric changes from 40 elements/130 items to 46 criteria/101 items. Diversity scoring changes from CV to normalized HHI, the selected retrieval configuration changes from BM25 to OpenAI embeddings, and verification distinguishes access errors from unsupported claims. The direct-quotation/Fair Use component described in v1 Appendix G.3 is no longer described in v3.

E1.justification: Both versions retain coverage of 50 HLE-derived report tasks across 13 domains. v3 adds an adversarial verification scenario using human-reviewed claims with negated meanings or altered numerical values (Appendix F.3, Table 16). The larger query-log sample does not itself establish broader report-task coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparison replaces Claude Opus 4.1 with 4.5, replaces Gemini Pro with Flash for the fast setting, and removes Gemini think+search. Claim extraction compares GPT-5 and GPT-5-mini instead of GPT-4.1 and GPT-5-mini. v3 also compares OpenAI embedding retrieval against BM25. These revise comparator sets across several experiments; the sliding-window comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported query-log sample changes from 5,045 to 5,842, and Figure 3(b) changes from two sampled tasks per domain to all tasks. Rubric and diversity metrics change, verification ablations switch to GPT-5-mini, and new experiments vary retrieval, reasoning effort, and context size. Human correlation now averages per-judge metrics, whereas v1 describes correlating averaged judge scores with human scores.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands verification analysis with a batch-size, reasoning-effort, retrieval-method, and Top-K study on original and adversarial claims (Table 16). It removes v1's class-specific classification diagnostics (Table 15). The backtracking-versus-sliding-window analysis on 131 claims is retained unchanged as v3 Table 15.

E5.justification: v3 Table 2 adds standard deviations across five evaluator models to human-correlation results previously reported as point estimates. Figure 3(b) also adds ± variability annotations, without clearly defining them. These are additions to uncertainty reporting, not evidence of additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: The main score table is extensively revised: Qwen3-235B fast's mean changes from 6.67 to 5.11 under revised scoring, so this is not a same-setting performance decline. The granular-rubric Pearson correlation changes from 0.53 to 0.62 and Krippendorff's alpha from 0.17 to 0.33; expert-guidance values remain 0.75 and 0.55. v3 adds adversarial results and removes v1's per-class classification results.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix F.4 replaces the CV-based diversity definition with normalized HHI and its score transformation, and explicitly defines count-to-score normalization. The backtracking and hierarchical averaging equations remain equivalent apart from notation. No new theoretical guarantee or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain an expert-grounded taxonomy, fixed rubrics, task-specific guidance, and report-wide information verification. v3 updates the claimed rubric resource from 130 to 101 items. Its conclusion also drops v1's explicit assertion that systems lag behind human experts, focusing instead on shortcomings in request fulfillment and analytical soundness.

C2.justification: v1 characterizes granular rubrics as worsening evaluator reliability and dense extraction with small batches as essential. v3 interprets granular rubrics as producing a slight reliability recovery, finds that greater extraction density need not improve coverage, and favors batch 20 for efficiency. Appendix F additionally identifies severe verification-label imbalance and interprets the new adversarial tests. The original limitations paragraph remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds substantial reproducibility information: actual model/service configurations, evaluator identities and costs, human rating instructions, taskwise correlation and tie handling, metric normalization, and detailed prompt templates. It also adds a DEER repository link. These fill gaps in v1, whose promised baseline-configuration appendix instead contains benchmark comparisons; newly disclosed details alone do not establish procedural changes.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds RigorousBench and concurrent-work positioning, and revises capability comparisons, including recognizing implicit verification in ReportBench and DeepScholar-Bench more fully than v1. Section 2 removes the dedicated claim-verification survey, including InFact, MAPLE, ALiiCE, and CiteEval, while adding Prometheus, Prometheus 2, and MT-Bench judging references. This materially changes the literature coverage and comparative positioning.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, related-work section, information-verification exposition, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Evaluation dimensions receive consistent new terminology, and residual DREX naming is corrected. The appendices are reorganized, with taxonomy foundations consolidated and dedicated baseline, human-evaluation, and prompt sections added.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn to show concrete rubric scoring and claim–source relationships. The taxonomy table moves to the appendix, rubric examples expand from one dimension to five, and new guidance, prompt displays, and an ablation table are added. Heatmaps gain revised labels and variability annotations, and the document adopts a different page format with extensively rearranged floats.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves reproducibility and the ability to assess its validation: Appendices F–I supply scoring rules, model configurations, human-evaluation calculations, and prompts that v1 largely omitted. Adversarial tests address the original verification set's severe class imbalance, while uncertainty reporting and revised ablation interpretations improve evidential clarity. Removing per-class diagnostics and leaving the rubric revision insufficiently explained are drawbacks, but the documentation and validation gains outweigh them.
